question: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.

raiseTranscript.text: My team switched from our internal wiki to a new documentation platform mid-project. I was uncomfortable because it meant redoing a lot of my recent work and learning the new tool quickly.
I blocked time to migrate my pages first, asked a teammate for a quick walkthrough, and then shared a short tip sheet with the rest of the team. It ended up being faster to search and update.
Still a bit annoying at first, but once I saw others using my tip sheet I felt better about it.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Switched wiki mid-project; redid own work
Blocked time, asked for walkthrough, shared tip sheet
Quote: "Still a bit annoying at first, but once I saw others using my tip sheet I felt better about it."
Follow-up: Asked how it felt after - acknowledged lingering discomfort but focused on local outcome
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate described moving from personal discomfort with redoing work to proactively migrating their pages and helping teammates. The concrete quote about sharing a tip sheet shows they turned the change into a small positive for their immediate circle. This matches junior expectations of owning individual work and learning from the shift rather than resisting it. The story stays local but demonstrates clear follow-through. Biggest strength is the quick move from resistance to action without needing heavy prompting.

lowerTranscript.text: We had to move to a new ticketing system. I didn't like it because the old one was faster for me.
I kept using the old system for a while until my manager told me to stop. Eventually I switched but it slowed me down.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
New ticketing system; resisted because old one was faster
Continued using old system until told to stop
Quote: "Eventually I switched but it slowed me down."
Follow-up: Asked what steps taken - showed compliance only after directive
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate only switched after being told to stop and framed the outcome as slowing them down rather than any learning or adaptation. No evidence of taking initiative to learn the tool or adjust their own workflow. This signals low ownership of individual change, which is a core junior expectation. The story lacks any proactive step or reflection on discomfort. Biggest gap is waiting for external direction instead of driving their own adjustment.

raiseTranscript.text: Engineering decided to adopt a new service mesh across two teams I worked with. I was uncomfortable because it added latency concerns for my service and required cross-team coordination I hadn't led before.
How did you handle the coordination?

I set up a shared doc with the other team, ran a small spike to measure impact on my service, and proposed a phased rollout that addressed their concerns too. We launched without the latency issues I feared.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Service mesh adoption across two teams; latency and coordination concerns
Shared doc, ran spike, proposed phased rollout
Quote: "We launched without the latency issues I feared."
Follow-up: Asked about coordination - showed influence across teams
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate moved from discomfort over cross-team coordination and technical risk to running a spike and driving a phased plan that satisfied both teams. The outcome quote shows measurable mitigation of their original concern. This demonstrates the expected senior ability to influence without authority and deliver cross-team impact. Story stays grounded with no inflated metrics. Biggest strength is converting personal discomfort into a concrete coordination mechanism.

lowerTranscript.text: We rolled out a new deployment process that affected my service. I was worried it would break things so I pushed back in the meeting.
Did you end up adopting it?
Yes, but only after the other team proved it worked on their side first. I still think it added unnecessary steps for us.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
New deployment process; pushed back due to breakage risk
Waited for other team to prove it before adopting
Quote: "I still think it added unnecessary steps for us."
Follow-up: Asked if they adopted it - showed delayed and conditional acceptance
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate's response was limited to pushing back initially and only adopting after another team validated the change. No evidence of leading coordination or exploring mitigations themselves. This falls short of senior expectations for influence across teams and turning discomfort into action. The final quote reveals lingering resistance rather than ownership. Biggest gap is absence of proactive steps to resolve the cross-team friction.

raiseTranscript.text: My team had to move from a feature-team model to a platform team model. I was uncomfortable because it meant losing direct feature ownership and needing to develop new skills in my reports.
How did you support the team?

I ran 1:1s to surface concerns, created a skill matrix for the new model, and paired stronger platform engineers with those who needed coaching. Two people who were initially resistant later led platform work.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Team model shift from feature to platform; lost ownership and skill gaps
1:1s, skill matrix, paired coaching
Quote: "Two people who were initially resistant later led platform work."
Follow-up: Asked how they supported the team - showed investment in people development
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate addressed their own discomfort by focusing on team development through 1:1s and a skill matrix, resulting in previously resistant engineers leading the new work. This aligns with manager expectations of creating leverage through the team and handling the people side of org change. The outcome quote provides clear evidence of raising others. Story remains realistic without heroic claims. Biggest strength is using personal discomfort as a prompt to invest in team capability.

lowerTranscript.text: We restructured the team to focus more on platform work. I told the team it was happening and asked them to adjust.
Some people left. The ones who stayed figured it out on their own.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Team restructure to platform focus; told team to adjust
Some left; others figured it out alone
Quote: "The ones who stayed figured it out on their own."
Follow-up: Asked about resistance - showed no active support or development
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate described announcing the change and leaving people to adjust independently, with attrition as the result. No evidence of coaching, skill development, or addressing underperformance constructively. This misses manager-level expectations around developing people and owning team outcomes during change. The quote highlights a hands-off approach rather than leverage. Biggest gap is treating the transition as purely structural instead of investing in the team's adaptation.

raiseTranscript.text: We decided to sunset a major product line that represented 30% of revenue. I was uncomfortable because it meant significant org change and potential talent loss at a time when we were already stretched.

I modeled three scenarios for talent reallocation and customer transition, then ran a series of all-hands and small-group sessions to surface concerns. We retained 70% of the affected engineers by creating new roles tied to the remaining products.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Sunsetting product line at 30% revenue; org and talent risk
Modeled scenarios, all-hands plus small groups, retained 70% engineers
Quote: "We retained 70% of the affected engineers by creating new roles."
Follow-up: Asked about trade-offs - showed strategic judgment and long-term thinking
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate framed discomfort around revenue and talent impact, then used scenario modeling and layered communication to retain most engineers through role creation. This reflects exec expectations of strategic trade-offs, org-level impact, and long-term thinking rather than heroics. The retention figure grounds the outcome without exaggeration. Story shows leverage through structure and communication. Biggest strength is converting a high-ambiguity decision into measurable talent retention.

lowerTranscript.text: We had to exit a business unit. I announced it to the leadership team and let them cascade the message.
How did you manage the talent side?
We offered standard severance. Some key people left but we backfilled over time.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of embracing a change that initially made you uncomfortable.
Exiting business unit; announced and cascaded
Standard severance; backfilled after departures
Quote: "Some key people left but we backfilled over time."
Follow-up: Asked about talent management - showed minimal strategic planning
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate limited their role to announcement and standard severance with no proactive talent strategy or scenario planning. This falls short of exec expectations for org-level impact and long-term judgment during major change. The outcome quote shows acceptance of key talent loss rather than mitigation. Story lacks evidence of trade-off analysis or leverage. Biggest gap is treating the exit as a one-time communication event instead of a multi-quarter talent and org transition.
